explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the doors. Nehemiah says, "When the wall had been rebuilt and I had set the doors in place…" (Nehemiah 7:1). A wall with a gap in it is just a very long suggestion. The doors are what finish the job.
Watchtowers sound very official, I'll give you that. But the text says Nehemiah "had set the doors in place" (Nehemiah 7:1). Towers never come up in this verse.

Cornerstones feel like a good guess for a building project. But this verse is about the wall already being rebuilt, and the next thing Nehemiah mentions is that he "had set the doors in place" (Nehemiah 7:1). No cornerstones here. Just doors.

That's the one. The verse says "the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed" (Nehemiah 7:1). Doors need somebody standing by them, or they're just fancy wood. The Levites were the men from the tribe set apart for service to God.

The builders just finished the wall, so I get why this one sounds right. But the verse names the ones appointed as "the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites" (Nehemiah 7:1). The building part is done. Now it's time for the keeping part.

Elders are a fair guess when a city needs leaders. But they aren't in this verse. The text says "the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed" (Nehemiah 7:1). Once the doors go up, somebody has to mind them.

explanations.answer: He was faithful and feared God more than most
explanations.explanation: That's right. Nehemiah says he put Hananiah, the commander of the fortress, in charge "because he was a faithful man who feared God more than most" (Nehemiah 7:2). Notice what he doesn't list: muscles, a big résumé or a fancy title. I'd have been picked for my mustache and been very wrong.

explanations.answer: He had fought off the enemies at the wall
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a good reason to hand somebody a city. But the text never says it about either man. It says Hananiah was "a faithful man who feared God more than most" (Nehemiah 7:2). That's the reason Nehemiah gives.

explanations.answer: He knew every family living in the city
explanations.explanation: Knowing everybody is a handy skill in a small town. But Nehemiah never says that about either man. He says Hananiah was "a faithful man who feared God more than most" (Nehemiah 7:2). That's what earned the job.

I see why this one's tempting, since most people open up early. But the text says the opposite. Nehemiah tells them, "Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot" (Nehemiah 7:3). That's late morning, not first light.

False is right. Nehemiah says, "Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot" (Nehemiah 7:3). Nobody is rushing out the door at sunrise in this city. The gates wait for the heat of the day.

Yes, the people who live there. Nehemiah says, "appoint the residents of Jerusalem as guards, some at their posts and some at their own homes" (Nehemiah 7:3). Imagine your neighbors on guard duty. I'd be the guy at my own house guarding the cookie jar.

explanations.answer: Soldiers sent by the king of Persia
explanations.explanation: Hired soldiers would be one way to do it. But the text doesn't mention any. Nehemiah says to "appoint the residents of Jerusalem as guards" (Nehemiah 7:3). The guards come from inside the city.

Tekoa is a real town in Judah, and its people did help with the wall (Nehemiah 3:5). But this verse picks someone else. Nehemiah says, "appoint the residents of Jerusalem as guards, some at their posts and some at their own homes" (Nehemiah 7:3).

That's it. The verse says, "Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it" (Nehemiah 7:4). Big wall, big city, not many neighbors yet. I know that feeling, because my drawer had lots of room and nobody in it.
A wall that big sounds like it should hold a crowd. But the verse says, "Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it" (Nehemiah 7:4). Lots of space, not lots of people.
Empty is close, but not quite. The verse says, "there were few people in it" (Nehemiah 7:4). Few means some folks were living there, just not many.
True, friend. The verse says "the houses had not yet been rebuilt" (Nehemiah 7:4). So there's a finished wall and a lot of open room, but the homes aren't back yet.
I get why you'd lean this way, since the wall is finished. But the verse says "the houses had not yet been rebuilt" (Nehemiah 7:4). The wall came first, and the houses were still waiting.

Right. The verse says God put it into Nehemiah's heart to gather the people "to be enrolled by genealogy" (Nehemiah 7:5). That means family lines, who came from whom. Nehemiah says it was his God who put it in his heart.
Counting money is a very human thing to do, I'll admit. But the text says the people were gathered "to be enrolled by genealogy" (Nehemiah 7:5). They were counting families, not coins.
Trade sounds like a good way to get a young city going. But that isn't what the verse says. The people were gathered "to be enrolled by genealogy" (Nehemiah 7:5). That's about family lines.

explanations.answer: The register of those who first returned
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Nehemiah says, "I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned" (Nehemiah 7:5). He wanted people enrolled by family, and the list was already written down. Some folks get a lucky find, and some of us just get a stale takeout menu.

explanations.answer: A letter from the king of Persia
explanations.explanation: Nehemiah did get letters from the king earlier (Nehemiah 2:7-9). But what he finds here is different. He says, "I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned" (Nehemiah 7:5).

explanations.answer: The scroll of the Law of Moses
explanations.explanation: The Law of Moses matters a lot, and it's coming up later in this story. But here Nehemiah says, "I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned" (Nehemiah 7:5). It's a family list, not the Law.

I see the thinking, since the city has room and a brand new wall. But the last verse says the people "settled in their own towns" (Nehemiah 7:73). They went back to their towns, not all into Jerusalem.

False is right. The text says the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants and the rest of the Israelites "settled in their own towns" (Nehemiah 7:73). Jerusalem stayed roomy while everybody went back to where their families belonged.
